stages.title: It is not coming from Netflix
stages.desc: When you press play, the video almost never travels from Netflix's own data centres to your TV.

stages.title: Two separate planes
stages.desc: Netflix splits the job in two: a control plane that decides things, and a data plane that moves bytes.

stages.title: You press play
stages.desc: Your app asks the control plane one question: where should I get this title from right now?

stages.title: It answers with a ranked list
stages.desc: The reply is not video. It is a manifest naming the nearest servers, sorted by measured latency.

stages.title: That server is a real box
stages.desc: Open Connect appliances are physical servers Netflix ships to internet providers, for free.

stages.title: Filled while you sleep
stages.desc: Every night Netflix predicts what your region will watch and pre-loads it onto that box.

stages.title: Then the bytes go local
stages.desc: Playback streams from inside your ISP, so the video never crosses the public internet at all.

stages.title: Why it feels instant
stages.desc: A few milliseconds away, already cached, and the quality adapts per chunk. That is the whole trick.

end.title: Netflix moved the internet closer to you
end.sub: Not a bigger cloud — thousands of small servers living inside the networks you already pay for.

post.caption:
Netflix does not stream from Netflix.

It ships physical servers into your ISP and fills them overnight, so the video you watch is already a few milliseconds away before you press play.
